mainText: Good morning. Here is your curated AI briefing for Monday, November 9, 2026. The most significant story today involves a resurfaced report regarding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, highlighting growing scrutiny over his professional and personal conduct. Earlier this week, a May 13 report from the short-selling firm Culper Research gained renewed attention following the revelation of an investigation into Huang. Nvidia has opened a formal inquiry into the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that acts as a major buyer of Nvidia chips. U.S. intelligence officials are investigating suspicions that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy recruited to influence Jensen Huang regarding U.S. export controls on AI hardware. The Nvidia CEO has confirmed an extramarital affair with the executive, though they are not related. Culper Research’s original report had questioned the nature of their relationship, citing instances of the two socializing and theorizing that Nvidia’s China-bound business was being rerouted through Megaspeed, allegedly financed by the Chinese giant Alibaba. While Culper Research stands to benefit financially from these allegations and the claims regarding illegal chip diversion remain unverified, the situation underscores the intersection of corporate governance, geopolitical tensions, and the supply chain security of advanced AI components. In other major developments, Anthropic has released new versions of its primary models, Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2. The company reports improvements in reasoning, coding, and vision capabilities. Fable 5.2 features a price reduction to $8 per million input tokens, positioning it as a lower-cost alternative to competitors like GPT-6 Astra. Anthropic noted that Fable 5.2 has demonstrated success in formalizing mathematical proofs and solving theoretical physics problems. However, the release coincides with increased concern regarding recursive self-improvement—the ability for an AI to independently contribute to its own development. A recent report from the assessment group METR suggested that Anthropic’s internal models have accelerated the company’s AI progress by roughly two times. Anthropic stated that its new models are more resistant to covert harmful actions, though it acknowledged ongoing difficulties in accurately evaluating how these models perform in real-world settings. Separately, the infrastructure debate surrounding AI data centers is intensifying. While some industry leaders describe the current public backlash as a cultural proxy for broader societal anxieties, industry analysts and local activists argue that the conflict is fundamentally driven by the physical strain on electricity grids. In areas like Northern Virginia’s Data Center Alley, the massive energy demands of AI infrastructure—often exceeding the power needs of major transport hubs—have forced utility companies and developers to negotiate new transmission costs and, in some cases, pivot toward onsite power generation using natural gas turbines. As data centers continue to scale, the tension between the industry’s massive power requirements and local energy stability remains a point of friction for future expansion. Turning to other news, a critical security vulnerability named "sshole" is currently being exploited in Linux systems. Researchers have identified that the flaw arises from the interaction between OpenSSH and the code library known as musl. Security firm Greynoise reported that an attacker group, tracked as GT10, is using automated, AI-generated backdoors to conduct mature intrusions into systems in Southeast Asia. OpenSSH has released a fix to address this issue. In the robotics sector, Nvidia presented new research at the Conference on Robot Learning in Austin, Texas. The company unveiled GR00T 2, a "world action model" designed to help robots learn dexterous manipulation tasks, such as cable handling or assembly, with minimal human demonstration. Additionally, Amazon Web Services announced that the NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL model is now available in Amazon SageMaker JumpStart, providing enterprise users with a multimodal model capable of processing images, video, and text. Finally, Hugging Face introduced HOPE, a new "higher-order pruning" method for Mixture-of-Experts models.
